questions.question_text: Given T > M ≥ N = O > P ≥ Q, what is the status of the claim M ≥ P?
questions.explanation: The chain T > M ≥ N = O > P ≥ Q entails M ≥ P; the strict and non-strict links are preserved in the transitive comparison.
questions.source: Inequality 01_ Class Notes.pdf, page 5; exam/year not stated

questions.question_text: Given T > M ≥ N = O > P ≥ Q, what is the status of the claim O > M?
questions.explanation: The chain T > M ≥ N = O > P ≥ Q entails the opposite comparison, so O > M cannot hold.
questions.source: Inequality 01_ Class Notes.pdf, page 5; exam/year not stated

questions.question_text: Given 1 < 4 ≤ 7 ≤ 3 = 5, assess conclusions I: 4 ≥ 5 and II: 1 < 5.

options.C: Both conclusions I and II follow

questions.explanation: The chain gives 4 ≤ 5, so 4 ≥ 5 is not entailed. It also gives 1 < 4 ≤ 5, hence 1 < 5 follows.
questions.source: Inequality 01_ Class Notes.pdf, page 6; exam/year not stated

questions.question_text: Given A ≥ B > C = D and C ≥ P ≥ E < T, assess I: A > E and II: A > T.

options.C: Both conclusions I and II follow

questions.explanation: A > B > C = D and C ≥ P ≥ E establish A > E. T is only known to exceed E; its relation to A is undetermined, so A > T does not follow.
questions.source: Inequality 01_ Class Notes.pdf, page 7; exam/year not stated

questions.question_text: Given S < C ≤ R = E > A ≥ M, assess I: S < E and II: R > M.

options.C: Both conclusions I and II follow

questions.explanation: S < C ≤ R = E entails S < E. Also R = E > A ≥ M entails R > M. Both conclusions follow.
questions.source: Inequality 01_ Class Notes.pdf, page 8; exam/year not stated

questions.question_text: Given B ≥ L = K < T = J, assess I: J ≥ B and II: J > L.

options.C: Both conclusions I and II follow

questions.explanation: J = T > K = L proves J > L. B ≥ L does not establish whether J ≥ B, so conclusion I is undetermined.
questions.source: Inequality 01_ Class Notes.pdf, page 9; exam/year not stated

questions.question_text: Given A ≤ M < Y; G < L > A ≥ D > I = N, assess I: G > N and II: L > N.

options.C: Both conclusions I and II follow

questions.explanation: L > A ≥ D > I = N establishes L > N. G < L alone does not compare G with N, so conclusion I is unknown.
questions.source: Inequality 01_ Class Notes.pdf, page 10; exam/year not stated

questions.question_text: Given C < R = E ≤ D; D = O < W ≤ N > U ≥ T, assess I: C < W and II: W ≥ T.

options.C: Both conclusions I and II follow

questions.explanation: C < R = E ≤ D = O < W proves C < W. Although N > U ≥ T, W ≤ N does not determine W versus T; II is not entailed.
questions.source: Inequality 01_ Class Notes.pdf, page 11; exam/year not stated

questions.question_text: Statements: A > B and C > D. Conclusions I: A > C; II: D > A. Which conclusion set follows?

options.C: Both conclusions I and II follow

questions.explanation: The two chains are disconnected. Assignments can reverse either proposed cross-chain comparison, so neither conclusion is definitely true.
questions.source: Original SSC-style practice question

questions.question_text: Statements: X ≥ Y > Z = W. Conclusions I: X > W; II: Y > Z. Which conclusion set follows?

options.C: Both conclusions I and II follow

questions.explanation: X ≥ Y > Z = W makes X > W by transitivity, and Y > Z is a stated strict link. Both follow.
questions.source: Original SSC-style practice question

questions.question_text: Statements: P > Q ≥ R. Conclusions I: P > R; II: R ≥ P. Which conclusion set follows?

options.C: Both conclusions I and II follow

questions.explanation: P > Q ≥ R entails P > R. The reverse R ≥ P contradicts this strict ordering, so only I follows.
questions.source: Original SSC-style practice question

questions.question_text: Statements: A ≥ B > C. Conclusions I: C ≥ A; II: A > C. Which conclusion set follows?

options.C: Both conclusions I and II follow

questions.explanation: A ≥ B > C entails A > C. C ≥ A is impossible under that strict transitive relation; only II follows.
questions.source: Original SSC-style practice question

questions.question_text: With no relation given between X and Y, conclusions I: X > Y and II: X ≤ Y form an exhaustive, mutually exclusive pair. What follows?

options.C: Both conclusions I and II follow
options.D: Either conclusion I or II follows

questions.explanation: For any ordered values exactly one of X > Y or X ≤ Y is true. Neither is individually entailed without premises, but the complementary pair is exhaustive and exclusive.
questions.source: Original SSC-style practice question

questions.question_text: In this coded system, @ means >, # means ≥ and $ means =. Statements: A @ B, B # C, C $ D. Conclusions I: A > D; II: B ≥ D. Which conclusion set follows?

options.C: Both conclusions I and II follow

questions.explanation: Decode the symbols: A > B ≥ C = D. Transitivity gives A > D and B ≥ D; both conclusions follow.
questions.source: Original SSC-style practice question

questions.question_text: In this coded system, ! means <, ~ means ≤ and = means equality. Statements: P ! Q, Q ~ R, R = S. Conclusions I: P < S; II: R > Q. Which conclusion set follows?

options.C: Both conclusions I and II follow

questions.explanation: Decode as P < Q ≤ R = S, so P < S follows. Q ≤ R permits equality; therefore R > Q is not guaranteed.
questions.source: Original SSC-style practice question

questions.question_text: Statements: A > B and C = D. What is the status of the relationship A > C?
questions.explanation: A and B form one component, while C = D forms another. Values can satisfy the statements with A > C or A ≤ C, so the relationship cannot be determined.
questions.source: Original SSC-style practice question

questions.question_text: Statements: L ≥ M > N = O; O > P ≥ Q. Conclusions I: L > P; II: M > Q. Which conclusion set follows?

options.C: Both conclusions I and II follow

questions.explanation: M > N = O > P ≥ Q entails M > P ≥ Q and hence M > Q. Since L ≥ M > P, L > P also follows.
questions.source: Original SSC-style practice question
